cur:monumental-santa-maria-in-domnica-ap.summary: The Virgin, dressed in dark blue and seated on a jewelled throne, holds the Christ Child on her lap; he raises his hand in blessing and holds a scroll. A multitude of angels with haloes crowds around them in rows, and Pope Paschal I, with the square halo of the living, kneels at the Virgin's feet and touches her red slipper. The mosaic is one of the most intimate images of papal devotion to the Mother of God in early medieval Rome.
facts: The apse mosaic was commissioned by Pope Paschal I (817–824); his monogram appears above the Virgin's head.
Above the apse, the arch shows Christ between two angels with the twelve apostles, and Moses and Elijah below.

cur:objects2-princeton-censer-new-testam.summary: Around the bowl of this bronze censer runs a frieze of Gospel scenes, identified by the museum as the Annunciation, Nativity, Baptism, Crucifixion and the Women at the Sepulchre, the great feasts of Christ's life from Incarnation to Resurrection. As incense smoke rose through the church, the swinging vessel displayed the whole story of salvation.
facts: Kurt Weitzmann published this piece as 'An East Christian censer' in the Record of the Princeton museum.
It belongs to a group of bronze censers with reliefs of the life of Christ catalogued by Ilse Richter-Siebels in her 1990 study of 'Palestinian' censers.

met:447998.summary: On the round disc of this red earthenware oil lamp, the haloed Christ stands holding a cross-staff, treading underfoot the lion, the dragon, the asp and the basilisk, while angels fly at either side; christograms in circles and chevrons decorate the rim. Small mould-made lamps like this were the everyday light of early Byzantine North Africa, and the image of Christ victorious over evil was thought to protect the lamp's owner.
facts: The Met notes that such lamps were made from double moulds and burned castor or sesame oil with a wick of plant fibre or linen.
The four beasts come from the Latin text of Psalm 91 (90):13, read in the early Church as Christ's triumph over Satan.
Christ treading on the beasts was a variant of the 'Christ in Triumph' image of the risen Christ, found in Late Antique and early medieval art but never common.
